overview.title: From NLP history to preparing text: tokens and regex splitting
overview.main_topic: Why text has to be turned into numbers, the choice between character- and word-level representations, and splitting text into tokens with a regular expression
overview.central_idea: Neural networks consume tensors of numbers, but text is a string of symbols with no single natural numeric form. Every text pipeline therefore starts with a splitting step that cuts text into small units called tokens; regular expressions are a flexible tool for doing this, starting with the simplest pattern "." that splits a string into characters.
overview.importance: This page closes the historical overview of NLP (section 14.1) and opens the practical part of the chapter. The tokenization ideas introduced here (characters vs. words, splitting, later indexing and vocabularies) underlie every text model in chapters 14 and 15, from bag-of-words classifiers to the Transformer.
learning_objectives: Explain why raw text cannot be fed directly into the deep learning models of earlier chapters
Contrast character-level and word-level numeric representations of text
Define a token and the splitting (tokenization) step
Read the regex "." and the function split_chars that uses re.findall to split a string into characters
Summarize the authors' caution about attributing human-like intelligence to large language models
prerequisites: Tensors as the numeric input of neural networks (chapter 2)

summary:
The page opens with the end of section 14.1's historical survey. The authors finish a thought begun on p.407 about modern large language models: despite our tendency to see intelligence in "things that talk," these models **copy and synthesize training data** in a way that is wholly distinct from, and much less efficient than, human intelligence. Yet they concede that the emergence of complex behaviour from a training setup as simple as "guess the missing word" is one of the most shocking empirical results of the last decade of machine learning. They then preview the next three chapters: skipping the hand-coded linguistic features that dominated until the 1990s, they will cover everything from logistic-regression text classifiers to LSTMs for translation, and examine closely why the Transformer is so scalable and generalizes so well on text.

**Section 14.2, Preparing text data**, starts with the example sentence `The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog.` The obstacle is that this input is **not numeric**, while every technique from previous chapters needs tensors of numbers. Images have a fairly natural numeric form (pixel intensities), but text can be encoded numerically in several ways.

Two intuitive options are offered:

- a **character-level** representation, borrowing from text file encodings such as ASCII: chop the input into characters and give each a unique index;
- a **word-level** representation: break sentences apart on spaces and punctuation and map each word to a unique number.

Both are reasonable, and both share a step present in all text preprocessing: **splitting** the text into small units called **tokens**. Regular expressions are introduced as a powerful splitting tool because they can flexibly match patterns of characters. The most basic regex, `"."`, matches any single character, so `re.findall(r".", text)` returns the list of characters. The page ends just before the function is applied to the example sentence (shown on p.409).

paragraphs.excerpt: recognition machines. Despite our persistent human tendency to find intelligence in “things that talk,”
paragraphs.what_it_says: Completing a sentence from p.407 (modern language models are described as pattern-recognition machines), the authors say that despite our tendency to find intelligence in things that talk, these models copy and synthesize their training data in a way wholly distinct from, and much less efficient than, human intelligence. They also admit that complex behaviour emerging from the simple "guess the missing word" training setup has been one of the most shocking empirical results of the past decade.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The authors hold two views at once. Language models are not minds: they are statistical machines that recombine what they saw in training, and they need vastly more data than a human to reach comparable fluency. Even so, it was not obvious beforehand that next-word or missing-word prediction at scale would produce abilities such as translation, summarization or question answering, and that surprise is real.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It sets realistic expectations for the chapter. The text models built in chapters 14-15 are pattern recognizers over token statistics, which matches p.407's statement that the models in this book "won't possess a human-like understanding of language." It also explains why the simple language-modelling objective gets so much attention in chapter 15.
paragraphs.technical_idea: "Guess the missing word" covers both causal language modelling (predict the next token) and masked language modelling (predict a hidden token from both sides), which the book later discusses for BERT on p.479.

terminology.meaning: Capabilities that appear in a trained model without being explicitly specified in its objective, here arising from simple word-prediction training at large scale.
The authors' informal name for self-supervised language-modelling objectives in which the model predicts held-out tokens of real text.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The authors preview the coming chapters on text. The progression runs from simple set-based models, to sequence models (RNNs and LSTMs), to attention-based Transformers.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives the reader a map: the tokenization and vectorization tools introduced next are reused by every model in that progression.

paragraphs.excerpt: There is an obvious blocker before we can start applying any of the
paragraphs.what_it_says: Using the example sentence "The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog.", the authors point out that the input is not numeric. Before any modelling we must translate written words into tensors of numbers. Unlike images, which have a relatively natural numeric representation, text can be represented numerically in several ways.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A neural network is a chain of tensor operations (dot products, additions, activations), so it can only work on numbers. An image already is a grid of numbers, pixel intensities per channel. Text is a sequence of discrete symbols, and nothing forces one particular mapping to numbers: you have to choose the units (characters, words, subwords) and how to number them.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the motivation for the whole of section 14.2. The choices made in text preprocessing (unit size, vocabulary, standardization) strongly affect what the model can learn and how big it is.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book): this example sentence is a well-known English pangram (it is usually written "jumps", not "jumped"), so it is convenient for character-level examples because it contains every letter.

terminology.meaning: A mapping from raw data (here, text) to numbers or tensors that a model can process.
A multidimensional array of numbers, the data structure that neural networks consume.

paragraphs.excerpt: A simple approach would be to borrow from standard text file formats
paragraphs.what_it_says: Two simple schemes are proposed. One borrows from standard text file formats and uses something like ASCII: chop the input into characters and assign each a unique index. The other is word-based: break sentences apart on spaces and punctuation, then map each word to a unique number.
paragraphs.what_it_means: These are the two classic granularities of tokenization. Character-level uses a tiny alphabet but long sequences, and each unit carries little meaning. Word-level gives shorter sequences of more meaningful units, but needs a very large vocabulary and has trouble with words it has never seen.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The trade-off between the two motivates subword tokenization, covered in section 14.2.2 (p.414), which sits between them.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: ASCII assigns the integers 0-127 to English letters, digits, punctuation and control characters; Unicode extends this to more than a million code points, a scaling problem the book raises on p.409.

terminology.meaning: A 7-bit character encoding that assigns integers 0-127 to English characters, e.g. 'A' is 65.
Treating each character as a unit and giving it its own index.
Treating each word (split on spaces and punctuation) as a unit and giving it its own index.

paragraphs.excerpt: These are both good approaches to try, and in general, all text
paragraphs.what_it_says: Both approaches are worth trying, and all text preprocessing includes a splitting step in which text is split into small individual units called tokens. Regular expressions are a powerful splitting tool because they can flexibly match patterns of characters in text.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Whatever unit you pick, the first step of a text pipeline is the same: turn one long string into a list of pieces. Those pieces, tokens, are the atoms the model sees. Regular expressions let you state the splitting rule compactly ("any character", "a run of letters", "a punctuation mark").
paragraphs.why_it_matters: "Token" is the central term of the NLP chapters. Later the book counts sequence lengths, vocabulary sizes and model inputs in tokens.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Splitting (tokenization) is usually followed by indexing (token -> integer, p.409) and often preceded by standardization (lowercasing, removing punctuation, p.410).

One unit produced by splitting: a character, a word, a subword, or a punctuation mark.
A pattern language for matching sequences of characters in strings.

paragraphs.excerpt: Let’s look at how to use a regular expression to split a string
paragraphs.what_it_says: The authors show how to use a regex to split a string into characters. The most basic regex is ".", which matches any character in the input text. The code imports the regex library as re and defines split_chars(text), which returns re.findall(r".", text).
paragraphs.what_it_means: re.findall scans the string left to right and returns every non-overlapping match of the pattern as a list. Since "." matches exactly one character, every character (including spaces and the final period) becomes its own list element, which gives a character-level tokenizer in one line.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the smallest working tokenizer, and the word-level version on the next page is a small change to the same pattern-based approach.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: by default "." matches every character except a newline; a string with line breaks would lose them unless the DOTALL flag is used.

terminology.meaning: Returns a list of all non-overlapping matches of a pattern in a string.
Regex metacharacter matching any single character (except newline by default).

concepts.name: Tokenization (splitting)
concepts.definition: The preprocessing step that splits a text string into a sequence of small units called tokens.
concepts.intuition: Like cutting a sentence into Lego bricks: the model can only build from bricks, so first decide how big the bricks are and cut the text into them.
concepts.technical: A function from a string to a list of strings, e.g. via re.findall with a pattern. The token granularity (character, word, subword) sets vocabulary size, sequence length and how much meaning each unit carries.
concepts.significance: Every text model in the book starts with tokenization; the book says "all text preprocessing will include a splitting step."
concepts.misconception: Tokens are not always words: they can be characters, subwords or punctuation marks.

concepts.name: Token
concepts.definition: A small individual unit of text produced by the splitting step.
concepts.intuition: The atom of text that a model sees.
concepts.technical: Tokens are later mapped to integer indices through a vocabulary (p.409) and then to vectors (one-hot, multi-hot or embeddings).
concepts.significance: Lengths, vocabulary sizes and model inputs in the NLP chapters are all counted in tokens.
concepts.example: In split_chars, each character of "The quick brown fox..." (including spaces) is a token.
concepts.misconception: A space is not automatically dropped: with the "." regex, spaces become tokens too.

concepts.name: Regular expression
concepts.definition: A pattern language that flexibly matches sequences of characters in text; the book uses it to split strings into tokens.
concepts.intuition: A search template: "." means "any one character", so finding all matches of it lists every character.
concepts.technical: re.findall(pattern, text) returns all non-overlapping matches. The book imports the third-party regex package as re; it is largely a superset of Python's built-in re module.
concepts.significance: It gives concise, adjustable splitting rules; changing the pattern changes the tokenizer.
concepts.misconception: Beyond the book: "." does not match a newline unless the DOTALL flag is set.

concepts.name: Character-level vs. word-level representation
concepts.definition: Two ways to make text numeric: give each character a unique index (as ASCII does), or split on spaces and punctuation and give each word a unique index.
concepts.intuition: Characters are a small alphabet that produces long sequences; words are a big dictionary that produces short sequences.
concepts.technical: Character vocabularies are small (dozens to thousands) and have no unknown words, but sequences are long and each unit carries little meaning. Word vocabularies are large (tens of thousands or more) and give out-of-vocabulary words, but each unit carries more meaning.
concepts.significance: This trade-off drives the comparison in 14.2.1 and the subword compromise in 14.2.2.
concepts.example: The example sentence has 45 characters but 10 word-and-punctuation tokens.
concepts.misconception: Neither is always better; the book calls both "good approaches to try."

code.title: split_chars: a character tokenizer with regex
code.what_it_does: Defines a function that splits any string into a list of single-character tokens.

line_explanations.explanation: Imports the third-party regex package under the name re, so the code reads like Python's built-in re module.

re.findall(r".", text) returns every non-overlapping match of "." (any one character) in text, i.e. the list of all characters in order. The raw string r"..." stops Python from interpreting backslashes, which is good practice for regex patterns even though this one has none.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: a Python string. Output: a list of one-character strings, with spaces and punctuation kept. For the example sentence the first 12 items are shown on p.409.
code.algorithm: Scan the string left to right; each position matches "." and becomes one list element.
code.theory_link: Implements the character-level splitting step described on this page.

parameters.name: r"."
parameters.role: The pattern: any single character (except newline).

pitfalls: Beyond the book: newlines are not matched by "." by default, so they vanish from the output; use re.findall(r".", text, flags=re.DOTALL) or simply list(text) to keep them.
The regex package must be installed (pip install regex); with the standard library you could write import re instead, and this pattern behaves the same.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written illustration (not from the book)
import re
print(re.findall(r".", "dog."))          # ['d', 'o', 'g', '.']
print(list("dog."))                      # same result without regex
print(re.findall(r".", "a\nb"))         # ['a', 'b']  newline dropped
print(re.findall(r".", "a\nb", re.S))   # ['a', '\n', 'b']

deeper.title: Why images are "natural" and text is not
deeper.body: An image already **is** a tensor: height x width x channels, with intensities that have a meaningful order (200 is brighter than 100) and a meaningful neighbourhood (adjacent pixels are related). Text symbols have neither property. The index you give "fox" is arbitrary; "fox"=4 is not "half of" "over"=6. Text preprocessing has to choose (1) the unit, (2) an arbitrary but consistent numbering and (3) later a vector representation (one-hot, multi-hot, embeddings) in which arithmetic makes sense. This page deals with step (1).

deeper.title: Character vs. word tokens on the example sentence
deeper.body:
`The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog.`

- Character tokens: 45 (including 8 spaces and the period). The alphabet needed is small: about 28 distinct symbols here.
- Word-and-punctuation tokens (p.409's regex): 10, namely `The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog .`

So characters give sequences about 4.5x longer, while words need a vocabulary that grows with every new word in the corpus. (Counts computed for this note, not printed in the book.)

deeper.title: "Guess the missing word" as a training setup
deeper.body:
1. Take a large amount of raw text (no labels needed).
2. Hide a token: either the next one (causal LM) or a random one in the middle (masked LM, p.479).
3. Train the model to predict the hidden token from the visible ones.
4. Repeat billions of times.

The authors' point on this page is that such a simple objective, at scale, produced surprisingly complex behaviour, while the resulting models remain statistical pattern recognizers and not human-like minds.

misconceptions.claim: Large language models understand language the way humans do, because they talk fluently.
misconceptions.correction: The authors say these models copy and synthesize training data in a way wholly distinct from, and much less efficient than, human intelligence, even though their emergent abilities are surprising.

misconceptions.claim: There is one correct way to turn text into numbers.
misconceptions.correction: Unlike images, text "could build a numeric representation ... in several ways": character-level, word-level and (later) subword-level are all valid choices with trade-offs.

misconceptions.claim: Splitting with "." removes spaces and punctuation.
misconceptions.correction: "." matches any character, so spaces and the period are kept as tokens (p.409 shows " " in the output).

questions.explanation: In a regex, "." matches any single character, so every character, including the space and the period, becomes a token. The first option is word-level splitting, the third treats "." as a literal period (that would need \.), and the last wrongly drops the space and period.

questions.question: Why do the authors say images have a "relatively natural numeric representation" while text does not?
questions.answer: Images are already grids of pixel intensities, i.e. numbers. Text is a sequence of discrete symbols, and you must choose how to break it up (characters, words, ...) and how to number the pieces; several valid schemes exist.
questions.explanation: The page states that before modelling "we need to translate the written word into tensors of numbers" and that text can be represented numerically "in several ways."

questions.question: What is a token, according to this page?
questions.answer: A small individual unit that text is split into during the splitting step of preprocessing.
questions.explanation: The book defines splitting as the step "where text is split into small individual units, called tokens."

questions.question: Name the two representations proposed on this page and give one advantage of each.
questions.answer: Character-level (e.g. ASCII-like indices for each character): a small alphabet and no unknown words. Word-level (split on spaces and punctuation): each token carries more meaning and sequences are much shorter.
questions.explanation: The book proposes both and calls them "good approaches to try"; the advantages listed are an elaboration (the book develops the trade-off in 14.2.1-14.2.2).

questions.question: Which statement best matches the authors' view of modern language models on this page?
options: They reason like humans but more efficiently.
They copy and synthesize training data in a way distinct from human intelligence, yet their emergent behaviour is surprising.
They depend on hand-coded linguistic features from the 1990s.
They are no more capable than logistic regression.
questions.answer: They copy and synthesize training data in a way distinct from human intelligence, yet their emergent behaviour is surprising.
questions.explanation: The text says they are "wholly distinct (and much less efficient!)" than human intelligence, but their emergence from "guess the missing word" was "one of the most shocking empirical results." The first option contradicts "less efficient", the third contradicts the move away from hard-coded features, and the fourth contradicts the stated surprise.
